france24fr.description: Alors que le coup d’envoi de la Coupe du monde 2026 sera donné le 11 juin, qui sont les favoris pour soulever le trophée le 19 juillet ? L'Argentine, l'Espagne, la France, le Portugal, l'Angleterre, le Maroc, le Sénégal… Passage en revue des forces en présence.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : quand l'administration Trump complique le bon déroulement de la fête
france24fr.description: Un arbitre somalien refoulé à son entrée aux États-Unis, des spectateurs iraniens privés de billet : à deux jours de l'ouverture du Mondial 2026, la politique migratoire américaine cause déjà des tensions.

france24fr.title: Donald Trump, côte de popularité de Donald Trump au plus bas, hué à New York
france24fr.description: Quand la politique américaine s'invite dans l'arène sportive… Hier soir à New York, la présence de Donald Trump à une finale de la NBA ne semble pas avoir été appréciée par les supporters. Il a été hué lorsque son visage est apparu sur les grands écrans. Précisions de Ludovic de Foucaud suivi de l’analyse de Matthieu Mabin, correspondant de France 24 à Washington.

france24fr.title: EXCLUSIF : Nous avons pu entrer dans un bastion du Hezbollah fermé aux journalistes
france24fr.description: Les échanges de tirs entre le Hezbollah et Israël se poursuivent. Dimanche, Tsahal a de nouveau frappé le quartier de la Dahiyeh, au sud de Beyrouth, contrôlé par le Hezbollah. Les bombardements ont fait deux morts et vingt blessés, dont quatre enfants. Nos envoyées spéciales Elena Volochine, Antonia Kerrigan et Hala Moukaddem ont pu obtenir l'autorisation du Hezbollah pour se rendre sur place, alors que le quartier était fermé aux journalistes. Reportage exclusif.

france24fr.title: Les "Ghetto Kids" impatients de danser avec Shakira pour la finale du Mondial
france24fr.description: Les danseurs de la troupe des "Ghetto Kids", composée d'enfants des rues d'Ouganda, s'apprêtent à danser avec Shakira lors du show de la mi-temps de la Coupe du monde de football. La mégastar colombienne les a invités à la rejoindre après que la troupe ait posté une vidéo de danse sur une de ses musiques.

france24fr.title: Affaire Lyhanna : que contient la "loi intégrale" contre les violences sexuelles ?
france24fr.description: Après la mort de Lyhanna, députés et associations ont réitéré leur demande pour que la France se dote d'une loi globale sur les violences sexuelles à l'encontre des femmes et des enfants. Leur appel semble avoir été entendu par le Premier ministre : il dit vouloir prendre de nouvelles mesures législatives. Que contient ce projet de loi? Réponse avec Marc Paupe.

france24fr.title: Gérald Darmanin dénonce "de graves dysfonctionnements" dans l'affaire Lyhanna
france24fr.description: Face à l'émotion immense suscitée par la mort de la jeune Lyhanna, la pression s'accentue sur le gouvernement. Après le courroux exprimé dans plusieurs villes de France par plus de 60 000 manifestants lundi soir contre les dysfonctionnements dans cette affaire, des plaintes vont être déposées contre l'État et contre le Garde des Sceaux. Gérald Darmanin a été entendu ce matin par les sénateurs dans le cadre de cette affaire, au côté du ministre de l'Intérieur. Récit de Noémie Roche.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 : un arbitre somalien écarté après s'être vu refuser l'entrée aux États-Unis
france24fr.description: L'arbitre somalien Omar Artan, refoulé samedi à son entrée aux États-Unis, n'officiera pas durant la Coupe du monde de football devant débuter jeudi, a annoncé la Fédération internationale de football à l'AFP lundi. Les raisons du refoulement d'Omar Artan, qui a notamment arbitré en Coupe d'Afrique des nations, ne sont pas connues.

france24fr.title: RDC : l'interdiction de vols commerciaux en Ituri prolongée
france24fr.description: En République Démocratique du Congo, l'épidémie d'Ebola continue à faire rage. Les derniers chiffres officiels font état de 515 cas confirmés, dont 91 décès. france24fr.title: Mali : certaines motos interdites pour lutter contre les jihadistes

Les autorités de transition expliquent cette décision par la nécessité de lutter contre les groupes armés. Cette interdiction va toutefois bouleverser le quotidien de nombreux Maliens, pour qui la moto reste un moyen de transport indispensable.

france24fr.title: Un agent des renseignements français au Mali condamné à 20 ans de prison
france24fr.description: Au Mali, un agent des renseignements français a été condamné à 20 ans de prison. Il a été reconnu coupable d’atteinte à la sûreté de l’État. Arrêté en août 2025, il est accusé de conspiration contre les institutions maliennes.

france24fr.title: Mondial 2026 en direct : favoris, joueurs à suivre, Donald Trump... Tout ce qu'il faut savoir
france24fr.description: À quelques jours du coup d'envoi de la Coupe du monde de football, France 24 vous propose un direct spécial pour décrypter les enjeux de la compétition. Qui sont les favoris ? Les investissements dans les pays émergents ne constituent plus un pari risqué. En Chine et en Inde, notamment, une nouvelle maturité économique se fait jour, qui pourrait surpasser l’Occident en termes de dynamisme et d’innovation

La situation a bien changé. Autrefois, les investissements dans les pays émergents constituaient un pari risqué sur la croissance rapide de quelques rares économie

phys-org.title: How waves, ponds and green algae are accelerating sea ice melt in Antarctica
phys-org.description: Picture sea ice in your mind. You probably imagine brilliant white, snow-covered floes floating on the surface of the ocean, home to penguins in the south of the globe or polar bears in the north.

phys-org.title: New dating of Spain's Sala Keimada rock art sanctuary reveals thousands of years of continuous use
phys-org.description: The Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH) has participated in a study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports on Sala Keimada, one of the rock art sanctuaries in Cueva Palomera, the main cave of the Ojo Guareña Karst Complex (Merindad de Sotoscueva, Burgos, Spain).

phys-org.title: Savanna chimpanzees use tools for capturing and feeding on army ants, study shows
phys-org.description: Chimpanzees are the only great apes, apart from humans, that have adapted to living on savannas as well as in forests. However, it is not yet well understood how the harsh ecological conditions of the savanna—compared with those of the forest—affect the foods chimpanzees eat and how they obtain them. Now, a study led by the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain (IJGE) reveals for the first time the strategies savanna chimpanzees use to make tools and extract aggressive arm

phys-org.title: Consumers often make suboptimal loan prepayment choices
phys-org.description: When consumers pay down debt, many choose to put funds toward their oldest loans first—even when doing so may not make the most financial sense, according to recent research by Alicia M. Johnson, assistant professor of marketing at the Isenberg School of Management.

phys-org.title: Ancient ground squirrel droppings reveal Arctic's rich evolutionary history
phys-org.description: Ground squirrel droppings, preserved for millennia in the Yukon's deep permafrost, have yielded an enormous amount of environmental DNA from dozens of species of plants, insects, microbes and large mammals, offering detailed genetic information about an environment that no longer exists. It is among the oldest ancient DNA ever recovered and sequenced.

phys-org.title: Koala numbers crashed across Australia 100,000 years ago. Global glacial cycles are likely to blame
phys-org.description: It's surprising how easy it is to see a koala every day in Australia's major cities. The cute, gray marsupial can be found on T-shirts, hanging off people's bags and pencils, and decorating any decent souvenir shop. But seeing a real koala in the wild has become increasingly tricky in some parts of the country. The iconic marsupial is now listed as endangered in Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory.

phys-org.title: 'Super-connected' teenagers key to tackling violent crime, study suggests
phys-org.description: Young people with the most connections to other suspected offenders of any age are almost five times more likely to carry knives than the average youth suspect, according to a new analysis of more than 200,000 U.K. police records. This top 5% of "super-connected" children aged 10–18 are almost three times more likely to commit violent crime, seven times more likely to commit robberies and nine times more likely to be involved in organized crime than the wider youth suspect population.

phys-org.title: Teachers more likely to accept low AI grades than equivalent human grades, study finds
phys-org.description: Teachers were more likely to accept an overly harsh grade given to a student by AI than when the unduly low grade was handed out by a human. As AI is increasingly integrated into decision-making, concerns about AI errors are often countered by assurances that humans will oversee and check the algorithm's work.

phys-org.title: These underwater 'living pink rocks' help store carbon: Scientists just found four new species
phys-org.description: Rhodoliths may look like small rocks on the seafloor, but they are actually living algae that create habitats for marine life and contribute to long-term carbon storage. A new study found that the deeper, low-light waters off Japan's Tanegashima Island harbor a surprisingly distinct and diverse community of these living pink rocks, including four species completely new to science.

phys-org.title: Some drugs 'fail' because of unrealistic testing conditions, scientists discover
phys-org.description: A drug once dismissed as ineffective suddenly worked—when scientists tested it under more realistic conditions that mimic the human body. In this surprising new discovery, Northwestern University scientists uncovered a hidden rule of drug behavior. A medicine's effectiveness can change dramatically depending on the conditions inside our cells.

phys-org.title: New maps chart old-growth forests across Alaska and British Columbia
phys-org.description: Mature and old-growth forests are vital for biodiversity, carbon storage, cultural traditions and economic activity. But in Alaska and British Columbia, these rich resources have not been reliably mapped, leaving much unknown about what land is protected. Now, University of Oregon researchers are leading a comprehensive mapping effort that sheds light on the location, makeup and conservation status of old-growth forests across the region.

phys-org.title: Possible dark matter-deficient twins discovered in the Fornax Cluster
phys-org.description: Astronomers have identified a possible new example of one of the universe's strangest galaxy types: galaxies that appear to contain little or no dark matter. The newly studied pair, FCC 224 and FCC 240, on the outskirts of the Fornax Cluster, share several unusual traits with the only known pair of controversial dark-matter-deficient galaxies. The findings were uploaded to the arXiv preprint server on May 22.

phys-org.title: Chasing the ghost dog of the Amazon: New insights into a mythical canid
phys-org.description: For decades, the short-eared dog (Atelocynus microtis) has been considered one of the least-known carnivores in Latin America, and potentially one of the least-known canids in the world. Because of its highly secretive nature, acute hearing, and strong sense of smell, this cryptic creature has successfully avoided people, leaving biologists with very few direct sightings in the wild.

phys-org.title: Quantum memory surpasses classical limits for storing unknown quantum operations
phys-org.description: Quantum memories, systems that store and retrieve information leveraging quantum mechanical effects, can outperform classical storage systems on some existing tasks. Yet these promising memories could also complete operations that are very difficult or impossible for classical systems, including the storage and retrieval of so-called isometry channels.

phys-org.title: Space telescopes are now overwhelmed by satellite trails
phys-org.description: Unfortunately, there's more bad news to report on the clear skies front. A new paper, available on the arXiv preprint server from researchers at NASA's Ames Research Center, reports that 73.3% of images the agency's new SPHEREx space telescope collected between May and September of last year were contaminated by at least one artificial satellite trail. And it's only going to get worse from here.

phys-org.title: Dogs uncover invasive pests that experts missed in real-world vineyard tests
phys-org.description: At a Maryland vineyard, Debi Persing guided her Boston terrier, Xephyr, slowly down a row of grapevines. Vineyard workers and scientists had already identified several invasive spotted lanternfly egg masses hidden among the vines. They believed they had found them all. Then Xephyr stopped at a vine they had marked clear. The little dog sat and pawed at the plant insistently.

phys-org.title: A lack of sex held back life's diversity for millions of years, fossil study finds
phys-org.description: The way that Earth's first animals reproduced held back life's diversity for millions of years, until stress and competition led to the development of sexual reproduction, which in turn accelerated the pace of evolution.

phys-org.title: Policy recommendations in climate-related research often 'an afterthought', analysis finds
phys-org.description: Too often, policy recommendations in climate-related research are either an afterthought or stray too far into advocacy, a new analysis has found. Researchers led by the University of Cambridge conducted a systematic review of more than 3,000 scientific papers focused on climate change mitigation and found that recommendations on how to turn science into policy were either nonexistent, failed to account for uncertainty or were "wish lists" disconnected from the study's findings.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

undark.title: A Peptide, a Secretive Scientist, and a Debate Over Evidence
undark.description: Access to unapproved peptides like BPC-157 has become a cause célèbre for the MAHA movement. Undark contributing editor Sara Talpos digs into the untold history of BPC-157 and its long journey from the scientific margins to the center of a debate over U.S. drug regulation.

undark.title: Book Review: Within Our Cells, the Miracle of Constant Mutation
undark.description: Our cells are constantly mutating in a battle for the survival of the fittest that is raging inside us daily, Roxanne Khamsi writes in “Beyond Inheritance.” Many of these mutations are harmless, others are cellular deviants that lead to disease, and remarkably, some can actually self-correct.

undark.title: The Six-Week Postpartum Checkup Comes Too Late
undark.description: In the U.S., maternity care generally ends with a checkup scheduled six weeks after giving birth. This single doctor’s appointment may be efficient for billing and discharge protocols, but the timing reflects the structure of the health care system more than the reality of maternal recovery.

undark.title: Book Review:  The Case for Making Data-Driven Decisions
undark.description: In “Beyond Belief: How Evidence Shows What Really Works,” science journalist Helen Pearson profiles a group of people working in medicine and other fields who became leaders of the worldwide evidence movement, which encourages the use of data from rigorous research to direct treatments, policies, and plans.

undark.title: What the Hantavirus Story Reveals About Medical Mistrust
undark.description: The reaction to an outbreak of hantavirus on a cruise ship reveals a story about mistrust in medicine and public health. In the U.S., hantavirus disproportionately kills Native Americans. A doctor who works at a hospital on Navajo Nation writes that such mistrust always lands hardest on the most vulnerable.

undark.title: Book Review: The Mind-Boggling Science of Enormous Numbers
undark.description: In “Huge Numbers: A Story of Counting Ambitiously, From 4½ to Fish 7,” mathematician Richard Elwes shows off his love of all things numeric, and, in particular, shines a spotlight on some of the largest numbers humans have ever contemplated, and the much larger numbers that await those who seek them out.

undark.title: When Scientific Arguments Obscure Moral Ones, Democracy Suffers
undark.description: The Pentagon’s new vaccine policy values individual choice over public health. Which of these values should be prioritized is a legitimate subject for democratic debate. But when experts respond to moral arguments animating policy decisions by reiterating facts, it undermines debate and fuels divisiveness.

proj-syn.title: The AI Revolution Mirrors the Green Transition
proj-syn.description: The need for massive upfront investments and the likelihood of significant job displacement imply remarkable parallels between the AI buildout and the green transition. In both cases, the state has an important role to play in guiding market forces on behalf of the public good.

proj-syn.title: Where Is China’s Trillion-Dollar Trade Surplus Going?
proj-syn.description: Whereas China’s trade surplus used to be absorbed largely by the central bank and channeled into official reserves, it is now being redeployed by private actors in search of yield. This indicates China’s progress on financial deepening and underscores markets' increasingly central role in shaping the economy.

proj-syn.title: The Future of Development Finance Is Not Primarily About Money
proj-syn.description: Multilateral development banks have not kept pace with changes to the global financial environment. For middle-income countries like India, accessing knowledge and technology is now a bigger challenge than raising capital, which suggests that these institutions must rethink their operating model.

proj-syn.title: Nigeria’s Perilous French Gambit
proj-syn.description: Nigeria’s increasingly close relationship with France marks a departure from six decades of foreign policy aimed at reducing French influence in West Africa. An increasingly close relationship with a power that has long sought to undermine Nigerian influence in West Africa will benefit only politically connected business elites.

proj-syn.title: Autocracy Is Fueling Mexico’s Fiscal Deterioration
proj-syn.description: Mexico’s recent ratings downgrades are merely a symptom of a more serious malady: the ruling Morena party’s efforts to consolidate power permanently. To ensure the legal predictability foreign investors require, President Claudia Sheinbaum would need to confront Morena’s ideological legacy and, more importantly, its cartel ties.

proj-syn.title: The Trump Economy Is Bad News for Republicans
proj-syn.description: Donald Trump triumphed in the 2024 election by continually hammering on the Biden administration’s dismal inflation record. If his party gets shellacked in this year’s midterm elections, it will be because he has made Americans even worse off.

proj-syn.title: SpaceX Is the New East India Company
proj-syn.description: Although SpaceX is not about to rule over foreign subjects, as the chartered companies founded in the early modern era did, it, too, is operating beyond the reach of any sovereign. And like its predecessors, it has already accumulated immense powers that governments will struggle to reclaim.

proj-syn.title: The ECB Should Not Raise Interest Rates Yet
proj-syn.description: Against a backdrop of acute uncertainty, weak growth, subdued wages, and elevated market interest rates, monetary tightening is warranted only when there is convincing evidence that higher inflation is becoming entrenched. No such evidence has yet materialized in Europe.

proj-syn.title: When Markets Run on Empty
proj-syn.description: Markets are flying high despite geopolitical turmoil because a broad-based willingness to keep spending has been matched by an ability to keep doing so. But as more economic participants exhaust their means and rely on debt, a painful moment of truth will arrive—sooner rather than later if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

proj-syn.title: The Pope and the AI Profiteers
proj-syn.description: In his first encyclical, Pope Leo XIV rightly rejects the idea that markets alone can be trusted to shape society’s technological future. Recognizing that AI raises questions that prices and profits cannot answer, the Chicago-born pope has posed a direct challenge to Chicago School economics.

proj-syn.title: AI Must Not Encroach on Human Dignity
proj-syn.description: In a world captivated by technological advances, Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical seeks to shift attention away from the marvels and terrors of AI and toward the magnificence of humanity. The message that the technology lacks a “moral conscience” and is distinct from human cognition is necessary and welcome.

proj-syn.title: The Key Forces Now Shaping Markets and Geopolitics
proj-syn.description: Three major factors are likely to shape economic and geopolitical outcomes over the next several years: politically unconstrained AI development, a shift from the logic of globalization to zero-sum thinking, and heightened international tail risks. Much could go right, or at least as expected—until it doesn’t.

proj-syn.title: The Living Ghosts of Violent Radicalism
proj-syn.description: Following World War II, the most militant student movements emerged in the former Axis powers as a way to cope with previous generations' complicity. But while the Red Army Faction and others were haunted by memories of past crimes, today's young people have mostly forgotten, and a growing number think far-right politics are cool.

proj-syn.title: Using AI to Test Policy Language
proj-syn.description: Policymakers have long understood that language affects economic behavior, but until recently, there were few tools capable of systematically analyzing its effects. AI may now help close that gap, enabling officials to anticipate how framing and timing can move markets and shift public opinion.

proj-syn.title: Europe’s Competitiveness Bogeyman
proj-syn.description: Calls for European leaders to protect domestic industry from "unfairly" subsidized Chinese competition have lately grown louder. But while tariffs might offer temporary relief to a few sectors, they cannot restore Europe's technological leadership, industrial dynamism, or export competitiveness.

proj-syn.title: Putting American Science on a MAGA Leash
proj-syn.description: A draft rule from US President Donald Trump’s White House Office of Management and Budget would subject all scientific research funding to the whims of political appointees, further undercutting a pillar of American power. The goal is to foreclose any future that is plural, contestable, and beyond the president’s control.

proj-syn.title: How Measles Came Roaring Back
proj-syn.description: Bangladesh is facing soaring measles cases not because of a single localized failure, but because of years of systemic erosion. Ultimately, maintaining herd immunity against highly contagious viruses requires relentless attention to supply and demand, as well as to the broader social and institutional foundations of public health.

proj-syn.title: Pete Hegseth’s Dangerous Call to Arms in Asia
proj-syn.description: Much like it did in Europe, the Trump administration has called on US allies in the Indo-Pacific to increase military spending to 3.5% of GDP. But a defense buildup on this scale would jeopardize economic growth and regional unity, and could lead Southeast Asian countries to gravitate toward China’s strategic orbit.
